A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same three-expert sign-language translation framework, renamed from MultiStream-LLM to SignBind-LLM. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary materials support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original How2Sign translation and ChicagoFSWildPlus fingerspelling results, component ablations, temporal-alignment experiments, and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v3 reports original results on How2Sign, ChicagoFSWildPlus, and BOBSL, together with additional component, fusion, transfer, and linguistic analyses.

M1.justification: The expert-routing, CTC, gated-fusion, and LLM pipeline remains. v3 changes manual inputs from hand crops to full frames and changes the main-text gate from manual-only conditioning to concatenated manual/lip features (v1 Equation 10; v3 Equation 12). It also describes independent decoder training on generated gloss/text pairs instead of v1's final training on fusion outputs.

E1.justification: v3 adds training and evaluation on BOBSL, extending coverage from American Sign Language to British Sign Language and interpreted broadcast footage. YouTube-ASL, How2Sign, and ChicagoFSWildPlus remain in use.

E2.justification: Geo-Sign is newly included in the How2Sign comparison, having only been cited in v1. The new BOBSL comparison includes GFSLT, Sign2GPT, Albanie, Sincan, and Lost in Translation. Appendix B additionally compares concatenation/MLP and cross-attention fusion alternatives and multiple YouTube-ASL baseline configurations. The fingerspelling comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds zero-shot transfer and How2Sign-only training controls, standalone phoneme evaluation, and POS accuracy analysis. It drops BLEU-2/3 from the main benchmark comparison and no longer reports sequence-classification accuracy. Optimization is reported as AdamW rather than v1's Adam; most other newly supplied hyperparameters are disclosures, not established changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds fingerspelling, fusion, and sequencer removal ablations; standalone expert tests; alternative fusion comparisons; pre-training/transfer analysis; POS analysis; and label-length analysis. Qualitative cases are replaced and extended to BOBSL. Conversely, v1's quantitative comparison of random, frequency-based, keyword, and LLM glossing methods is removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional v3 results continue to use point estimates.

E6.justification: Reported How2Sign BLEU-1/BLEU-4 changes from 46.0/23.5 to 49.4/22.1, while ROUGE remains 41.2 and fingerspelling accuracy remains 73.2%. The no-lipreading BLEU-4 changes from 16.6 to 13.6. v3 adds BOBSL BLEU-4 of 6.8, zero-shot 8.3, How2Sign-only 13.7, and numerous analytical results. These are revised or newly reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a mathematical complexity comparison between O(T) gating and O(T²) cross-attention operations. Expanded CTC formulas mostly unpack losses already present in v1. Neither version presents a theorem or proof framework.

C1.justification: The central claim that specialized signing, fingerspelling, and lipreading experts improve translation through fusion remains. v3 extends the headline state-of-the-art claim to BOBSL and adds provision of generated pseudo-gloss and phoneme annotations for BOBSL and How2Sign as a contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning gating's suppression of irrelevant mouth signals, benefits of diverse pre-training, and the tradeoff between content-word accuracy and function-word reconstruction. Appendix C discusses instructional-domain bias, while Appendix E explains proper-name hallucinations and semantic drift through weak conditioning and LLM priors. v1's discussion was substantially narrower.

D1.justification: v3 adds exact glossing prompts, phonemization tools and fallback handling, parameter counts, fusion architecture dimensions, training schedules, LoRA configuration, hardware, computational costs, and decoding settings. These substantially expand v1's sparse implementation documentation. However, v3 contains conflicting descriptions of epochs, full fine-tuning versus LoRA, and training-time totals.

R1.justification: v3 adds related-work coverage including SAGE, SLTUNET, hierarchical feature alignment, and Lost in Translation, alongside component references such as DINOv2, Gumbel-Softmax, and LoRA. The underlying positioning remains the absence of explicit fingerspelling/lipreading integration in prior SLT systems; publication and bibliographic updates do not constitute additional scientific changes.

P1.justification: Beyond the title and model rename, v3 extensively rewrites the introduction and method, reorganizes the pipeline into numbered stages, and develops a structured appendix with a contents list and dedicated analysis and implementation sections. This is substantial narrative restructuring, not merely added experimental content.

P2.justification: v3 adds an opening modality illustration, redraws the architecture diagram, replaces the earlier routing visualizations with different translation displays, and introduces a POS heatmap and label-length plots. Comparison tables are restructured, and new appendix tables document analyses, configurations, and intermediate fused outputs.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves important components and fusion choices weakly tested and provides few implementation settings. v3's expanded component tests, direct fusion comparisons, BSL evaluation, transfer analysis, and explicit failure discussion substantially strengthen the evidence and make the method easier to assess. Removal of the glossing-method ablation and inconsistent training disclosures weaken parts of the revision, but do not outweigh these substantial gains in scientific support and transparency.
